How to find DSO's for newbie.

Use your least powerful eyepiece and look for

Andromeda nebula Orion nebula The Pleides (really better in binoculars but easy to find)

Start with the bright stars in a constellation and then go from there. Use your finder scope. Make sure it's aligned by using the moon or very bright stars.

After you do this look for the crab nebula and other open and globular clusters. That will get you started.

Thanks,

Hairy Larry

hairylarry has good tips. I'm really an amateur but I'd add a few things to his suggestions.

  • First lay off the caffeine on a night you're going to observe.
  • Learn to focus your telescope properly.
  • Learn to use averted vision.
  • Don't be embarrassed to use a hood or blanket over your head if you have bright lights around you.
  • A lot of time DSOs are more easily visible under less magnification; don't shoot for going for highest magnification every time.

Check out the program stellarium if you haven't already. Once configured for your location it makes it really easy to find what you're looking for. It even has a mode to show you what it would look like to find an object through your telescope with your specific lenses.

I'd recommend looking for the Messier objects. I'm in moderately light polluted skies and I can find most of them depending on the season. (nearly all on a crystal clear cold night)

I am speaking to undergrads, grads, or teachers in any sort of economics, finance, or business programs anywhere. I am just curious about what I can learn about the current state of thought in University systems across the world. Do your programs teach/lean more Keynesian or Austrian? Left-wing or Right-wing? Democratic, Republican, or Libertarian? Marxist or Capitalistic? Free market or Socialist? Or any other distinction you might want to express?

Not concerned with if you accept their beliefs or not, just curious as to what you have been taught.
What current schools of thought are mainstream in Economic Departments across the United States or World?

Most top U.S. schools teach fairly mainstream economics, and not too many (though there are some) professors who publish seriously have an obvious political bias in their work. A couple of the major journals are somewhat politically biased (some left, others right). George Mason University is well-known to be Austrian. I think most of the younger economists stay away from politics (again, there are several exceptions to this) since there's so much emphasis on publishing.

For many universities I think it depends on which department and field of study you are in. The applied finance researchers may have a completely different thought basis than the development economists. For example, I have a microeconomics professor (I love his classes) that is one of the few people that disputes the Quantity Theory of Money in favor of the "Backing Theory". He wrote the damn Wikipedia article on it. We can talk more about backing theory later. My point is that what makes a department great, in my opinion, is that not all the professors agree. Students need to get different perspectives instead of being pounded over the head with one line of thought. Overall, however, I think most schools default to Keynesian and slightly left-wing.

My professor said the solid majority of economics faculty in the US are New Keynesians.

He went on to say the distinction is mattering less and less as microfoundations and empirical modeling become more important every day.
